title: Hürriyet Kasidesi: title, date and publication
short: The 'Ode to Liberty' took final shape in 1876 and was printed in the newspaper Vakit on 2 June 1876; its original title was different.
body: The popular title 'Hürriyet Kasidesi' (Ode to Liberty) is not Kemal's own. Akün's encyclopedia article records that the poem took its final form during the Serbian and Montenegrin uprisings and was published in Vakit (no. 236, 2 June 1876) under the heading 'Besâlet-i Osmâniyye ve Hamiyyet-i İnsâniyye' (Ottoman Valour and Human Zeal). Gariper and Bayraktar add that its first couplets had appeared earlier in Hürriyet, the Young Ottoman paper Kemal and Ziya ran in London from 1868. It went quickly into school books and anthologies and drew many imitations (nazire). Tanpınar called it a kaside of heroism (hamaset kasidesi): it keeps the classical kaside's monorhyme and its long run of couplets, but it praises an idea, liberty, where the old kaside praised a sultan or a vizier.

sources.cite: Ömer Faruk Akün, 'Nâmık Kemal', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 32 (2006), pp. 361–378
Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Ahmet Hamdi Tanpınar, 19'uncu Asır Türk Edebiyatı Tarihi (Istanbul: Çağlayan, 1988), p. 374, as cited by Gariper and Bayraktar (2017)

title: Kaside form, rhyme and redif
short: Every couplet ends in the same sound, -etten: a rhyme in -et plus the redif (refrain suffix) -ten, 'from', kept through all 31 couplets.
body: A kaside is a long monorhymed poem in couplets (beyit) whose first couplet (matla) rhymes in both lines. Here the matla pairs 'selâmetten' and 'hükûmetten', and every later couplet's second line ends the same way: 'iânetten', 'kıymetten', 'mihnetten', down to 'gafletten'. The fixed final syllable -ten (the ablative case, 'from') is the redif; the varying -et before it (selâm-et, hükûm-et) is the true rhyme (kafiye). The ablative fits the poem's argument, which is built on contrasts of turning away from one thing towards another: from office, from servility, from captivity. Kemal kept the old form deliberately; the novelty, as Gariper and Bayraktar stress, is in the subject, not the mould.

sources.cite: Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpaklı (eds and trans.), Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997), introduction and glossary
Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Haluk İpekten, Eski Türk Edebiyatı: Nazım Şekilleri ve Aruz (Istanbul: Dergâh), chapters on the bahirs

title: Metre: hezec (mefâîlün × 4)
short: The lines scan in the hezec metre, four feet of mefâîlün (short-long-long-long) to the line.
body: Read in aruz, the line falls into four identical feet: Gö-rüp ah-kâ / mı as-rı mün / ha-rif sıd-ku / se-lâ-met-ten, each short-long-long-long (. − − −), the pattern called mefâîlün. Four such feet to the line, eight to the couplet, make the hezec-i müsemmen-i sâlim, the 'complete eight-footed hezec'. As often in Ottoman verse, some short open Turkish syllables have to be held long to fit the pattern (imâle), and izafet vowels are lengthened or shortened as the metre needs. The insistent, almost marching beat of the unbroken mefâîlün suits public declamation, and the poem was in fact recited and memorised by generations of students. The scansion here is offered from the text; check it against a prosody handbook.

sources.cite: Tevfik Rüştü Topuzoğlu, 'Hezec', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 17 (1998), pp. 302–304
Haluk İpekten, Eski Türk Edebiyatı: Nazım Şekilleri ve Aruz (Istanbul: Dergâh), chapters on the bahirs

title: bâb-ı hükûmet: 'the gate of government'
short: The opening couplet presents the speaker's resignation from state office as a protest against an age that has turned from honesty.
body: 'Seeing the rulings of the age had swerved from truth and soundness, we withdrew, with honour and good fortune, from the gate of government.' The first person plural is the Young Ottoman 'we'. The couplet recalls the moment in 1867 when Kemal and Ziya left their posts and fled to Europe, but Gariper and Bayraktar read it more broadly: the protest is aimed not at the state as such but at the corrupt officials who run it. 'Münharif' (Arabic munḥarif, 'deviated, turned aside') is a key word: the age itself has gone off course. 'Bâb' (Arabic bāb, 'gate') recalls the Bâb-ı Âlî, the Sublime Porte, seat of the grand vizier.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'münharif'
Abdullah Uçman, 'Ziyâ Paşa', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 44 (2013), pp. 475–479

title: halk, hizmet: serving the people
short: A new political idea in old words: those who think themselves truly human never tire of serving the people.
body: 'Halk' had long meant simply 'people, creatures'; here it is the public whom the state should serve. Gariper and Bayraktar argue that the poem brings the modern idea of 'the people' as a value into Turkish literature, setting halk against the officials who neglect it. 'Mürüvvet-mend' is a Persian-suffixed adjective from Arabic muruwwa, 'manly virtue, generosity': the generous man does not withdraw his help (iâne, Arabic iʿāna) from the oppressed (mazlûm). The couplet works as a definition of humanity by duty, the first of the 'principles' that Kaplan saw in couplets 1–14.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141

Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'iane'

title: cevher: the jewel that falls
short: A jewel does not lose its value by falling to the ground; so a nation despised has not lost its worth.
body: 'If the nation has been held in contempt, do not think its glory diminished; a jewel does not lose its value and worth by falling to the earth.' The couplet is a classical proof-by-image (the second line illustrates the first, a device called irsâl-i mesel, using a proverb-like example). 'Millet' is one of Kemal's charged words: Gibb noted that it had meant a religious community and was now made to stand for 'the nation' or 'the people'. 'Cevher' (Arabic jawhar, from Persian gawhar) means both jewel and essence, so the line also claims that the nation's essence is untouched by its present humiliation. The jewel returns in beyit 26.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. V, ed. E. G. Browne (London: Luzac, 1907)
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'cevher'

title: hâk-i vatan: 'the soil of the fatherland'
greek: Persian khāk 'earth, dust'; Arabic waṭan 'homeland'; khamīr 'dough'
short: The body is kneaded from the fatherland's soil, so becoming soil again on its road is no hardship.
body: 'Since the leaven of the body's dough is the soil of the fatherland, what grief if one becomes dust on the fatherland's road through torment and pain?' (The archive text spells the second 'hâk' without the circumflex, 'hak olursa'.) The image adapts the Qur'anic creation of man from clay to the new idea of vatan, so that dying for the country becomes a return to one's own matter. Gibb (whose History of Ottoman Poetry was published posthumously in 1907, edited by E. G. Browne) credited Kemal with raising 'watan' from a vague word between 'home' and 'birthplace' to the equivalent of French patrie. Gariper and Bayraktar describe the speaker here as a 'mystic of the fatherland'.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. V, ed. E. G. Browne (London: Luzac, 1907)

title: The dog and the merciless hunter
short: Those who help a tyrant are base; only a dog enjoys serving a pitiless hunter.
body: 'The helpers of the tyrant in this world are the base; it is a dog that takes pleasure in serving the merciless hunter.' 'Denâet' (Arabic danāʾa) is baseness; 'sayyâd' (Arabic ṣayyād) is the hunter. In divan poetry the sayyâd is usually the beloved, hunting hearts with the snare of her curls; Kemal turns the stock figure political, so that the hunter is the oppressive ruler and his willing servants are hounds. Gariper and Bayraktar read the couplet as another reason for the speaker's resignation: to serve such a government would be a dog's work. The dog comes back as 'kilâb-ı zulm', the dogs of tyranny, in the last couplet.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141

title: ittihâd and ihtilâf: unity and disagreement
short: Victory lies in the union of the nation's heart; mercy comes out of the disagreement of opinion in the community.
body: The couplet balances two Arabic verbal nouns: 'ittihâd' (union) of hearts gives victory, while 'ihtilâf' (difference of opinion) within the community (ümmet) brings blessing. The second line echoes a saying widely circulated as a hadith (its authenticity is disputed), that the disagreement of the community is a mercy, and turns it into an argument for free debate, a theme of Kemal's journalism. Uniting the hearts but freeing the opinions is close to the Young Ottoman programme of constitutional consultation (meşveret). Note the movement from 'millet' to 'ümmet' within the couplet: the national and the religious community are still held together.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Ömer Faruk Akün, 'Nâmık Kemal', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 32 (2006), pp. 361–378

title: şîr-i der-zencîr: the lion in chains
short: The chained lion is not to blame for not moving; let Fortune be ashamed before the able men it has left without a share.
body: 'It is no reproach to the lion in chains that it cannot step forward; let fortune in the heavens be ashamed before men of high resolve who are left without a share.' The Persian construction şîr-i der-zencîr (lion in chains) gives the first appearance of the poem's emblem of the nation: powerful but bound. Gariper and Bayraktar, quoting Göçgün's prose version, read the couplet as placing the blame for the nation's weakness on its rulers, not on the people. The lion is unchained in the final couplet, where he is called to wake.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141

title: ziyâ: the light kept from its height
short: If light is far from the summit of its rising, that is by force; nature should blush for talent left lying on the ground.
body: 'Ziyâ' (Arabic ḍiyāʾ, light) is far from the 'evc', the apogee or highest point of a heavenly body's course, a term from Ptolemaic astronomy; and 'rif'at' is height, exaltation. Its distance is 'ıztırârî', forced, not natural. Gariper and Bayraktar take the light as a metaphor for the nation's gifted individuals, who should shine on high but have been kept down. The astronomical image continues the attack on 'felek' (the sky, fate) in the previous couplet: the cosmos is shamed by the waste of human capacity (kabiliyet), a word that points to the Enlightenment vocabulary of talent and merit.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'felek'

title: 'We are that noble race of the house of Osman'
greek: Persian dūda 'family, house'; Arabic muḥammar 'reddened'; ʿashīra 'tribe'
short: Three couplets beginning 'Biz ol...' praise Ottoman lineage: blood-red with zeal, makers of a world empire from a single tribe.
body: Kaplan's division of the poem, as summarised by Gariper and Bayraktar, gives couplets 15–17 to admiration for Ottoman history. The anaphora 'Biz ol...' ('We are those...') is a fakhr, the self-praise of a tribe or hero inherited from Arabic poetry. 'Dûde' (Persian dūda, 'smoke, hearth, family') means a dynasty; 'muhammer' (Arabic muḥammar) is 'reddened'; 'hûn-ı hamiyet' is 'the blood of zeal'. The second couplet's famous line recalls the founding legend in which Osman's small tribe (aşiret) grew into a world-conquering state (cihangirâne bir devlet). The third prefers the earth of the grave to the earth of humiliation (hâk-i mezar / hâk-i mezellet), a pun on the two senses of hâk.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141

Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'hamiyet'

title: The poem's design and its critics
short: Kaplan divided the poem into principles, Ottoman glory, the poet's own defiance and liberty; the word hürriyet itself enters only here, at couplet 18.
body: Kaplan's analysis, as given by Gariper and Bayraktar, divides the 31 couplets into four groups: principles of high value (1–14); admiration for Ottoman history (15–17); fearlessness and the poet's own conduct (18–24); and liberty (25–31). It is worth noticing that the word 'hürriyet' first appears in beyit 18, 'the battle of freedom', so that the poem's title names its goal, not its starting point. Critics differ on its merit. It is often praised as the first important poem of the new content, but its long chain of maxims also invites the charge of rhetoric over poetry, and Tanpınar's label, a kaside of heroism, places it in a tradition of declamation rather than lyric.

title: The executioner's lasso and the chain of captivity
greek: Persian kamand 'lasso'; jān-gudāz 'soul-melting'; aždar 'dragon'; Arabic isāra 'captivity'
short: Even if the hangman's soul-melting noose were a dragon of wrath, it would still be a thousand times better than the chain of slavery.
body: 'Kemend' is the lasso or noose (in divan poetry, the beloved's curling lock); 'can-güdâz' (Persian jān-gudāz) is 'soul-melting'; 'ejder' (Persian aždar) is a dragon. A long Persian chain of genitives builds the most frightening possible image of death, only to dismiss it in the second line: the noose is preferable (müreccah) to the chain (zencîr) of captivity (esâret). Gariper and Bayraktar note that this is the first couplet of the liberty theme proper. The noose against the chain is also a contrast between a quick death and a long bondage.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'ejder'
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'esaret'

title: vezâret, sadâret: the vizierate and the grand vizierate
short: The least pleasure of suffering for his cause is higher than being a vizier or even grand vizier.
body: 'Let the torments and hardships I have borne on my path be remembered, for the least pleasure in them is higher than the vizierate, than the grand vizierate.' 'Sadâret' is the office of the sadrazam, the grand vizier, the highest post open to a subject. The couplet answers the opening one: the man who walked out of the 'gate of government' now says the highest offices are worth less than the pains of exile. Kemal had in fact been exiled to Famagusta in 1873, where he spent some thirty-eight months; he was later allowed to live on Midilli (1877) and was appointed its mutasarrıf in December 1879, so the poet who scorned office also served the state as a provincial governor.

sources.cite: Ömer Faruk Akün, 'Nâmık Kemal', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, vol. 32 (2006), pp. 361–378
Kadri Nazlı, 'Namık Kemal ve "Vâveylâ" Şiiri Üzerine Notlar', Uluslararası Sosyal Bilimler Dergisi (Çanakkale) 1/1 (2016), pp. 61–73

title: Vatan as a faithless, coquettish beloved
short: The fatherland has become like the faithless, teasing beloved of divan poetry, who never spares her true lovers the pains of exile.
body: 'The fatherland has turned into a faithless, coquettish darling who does not spare her sincere lovers the sorrows of exile.' Every term is borrowed from the ghazal: 'bî-vefâ' (faithless), 'nâzende' (coquettish, Persian nāzanda), 'tannâz' (teasing, flirtatious), the sincere lovers (sâdıkân-ı aşk), the pains of separation (gurbet). In divan love poetry the cruel beloved who makes her lovers suffer is a convention; Kemal makes the country itself that beloved, with a bitter irony, since the patriots' 'reward' is banishment. Gariper and Bayraktar link it to Kemal's own exiles. It is one of the clearest examples of old imagery serving new ideas.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Walter G. Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song: Ottoman Lyric Poetry (Seattle: University of Washington Press, 1985)
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'nazende'

title: The diamond of zeal
short: Zeal in the heart is like the essence of the diamond: it is not crushed by pressure or by weight.
body: 'Gayret' (Arabic ghayra) means zeal, effort, protective pride. The couplet compares it to the diamond (elmâs, from Greek adamas through Arabic almās), the hardest substance known, and plays on 'cevher' in both senses, jewel and essence ('cevher-i elmâs ... cevher-i gayret'). 'Şiddet-i tazyîk' (force of pressure) and 'te'sîr-i sıklet' (effect of weight) have a faint scientific colour, the vocabulary of physics newly entering Ottoman prose. Compare the fallen jewel of beyit 3: the nation's value survives a fall, its zeal survives crushing.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'cevher'

title: Liberty as the beloved's face
short: In the closing couplets liberty becomes a bewitching beloved: we escaped captivity only to become prisoners of her love.
body: 'What a sorceress you are, ah, O face of liberty! We became the captives of your love, though we were freed from captivity.' The paradox of the lover's willing slavery, a commonplace of the ghazal, now celebrates freedom. 'Dîdâr' (Persian dīdār) is the face, the sight of the beloved; 'efsunkâr' (Persian afsūnkār) is enchanting. The following couplets beg her not to veil her beauty from the community's eyes and call her 'yâr-ı cân', beloved of the soul. Gariper and Bayraktar note that liberty here takes a woman's image and becomes the highest value of the poem. Read with beyit 22, the poem divides the old figure of the beloved in two: the faithless fatherland and the faithful liberty.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141

Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'didar'

title: kilâb-ı zulm: the dogs of tyranny
greek: Arabic kilāb, plural of kalb 'dog'; ẓulm 'tyranny'
short: The beautiful plains where the lion once roamed have been left to the dogs of tyranny.
body: 'Kilâb' is the Arabic broken plural of kalb, dog. 'The graceful deserts where you roamed have been left to the dogs of oppression.' 'Nâzende sahrâlar' (graceful wastes) are the lion's old hunting ground, that is, the lands of the empire. The line returns to the dog of beyit 5, now in the plural: the officials who served the hunter have taken over the country. Gariper and Bayraktar read it as the ruling class whose tyranny the awakened people will end.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük, s.v. 'zulüm'

title: 'Wake, O wounded raging lion'
short: The famous last line calls the wounded lion, the nation, to wake from the sleep of heedlessness.
body: 'Wake, O wounded, roaring lion, from this sleep of heedlessness!' 'Jeyân' (Persian žayān) means raging, fierce; 'hâb-ı gaflet' is the sleep of negligence, a phrase from Sufi preaching, where 'gaflet' is forgetfulness of God, here forgetfulness of one's rights. The chained lion of beyit 13 is now wounded and asleep, and the poem ends not with a prayer for the sultan, as the old kaside did, but with a call to the people. The poem entered school books and anthologies soon after its publication, which helps explain why this last line is so widely remembered.

sources.cite: Cafer Gariper and Yasemin Bayraktar, 'Hürriyet Kasidesi'nin Değerler Dizgesi Üzerinde Kimi Belirlemeler', Yeni Türk Edebiyatı Araştırmaları 18 (2017), pp. 127–141
